newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Swedish govt seen headed for OM, bourse, VPC merger.
newsitem.headline: Swedish govt seen headed for OM, bourse, VPC merger.

text.p: The Swedish government's decision to pull out of central securities depository VPC is expected to pave the way for a merger of VPC, derivatives trader OM and the Stockholm bourse, analysts said on Wednesday.
OM and the bourse are already in merger talks and have said negotiations will be finalised before this summer.
"The government wants VPC to take part in the merger talks between OM and the bourse," Paul Hansson, analyst at Nordbanken, told Reuters.

In its April 15 spring budget proposal the government said it wanted parliament to allow it to sell its 50 percent stake in VPC and use the proceeds and another 500 million crowns for investments in the financial infra-structure.
"It cannot be ruled out that VPC might be included in a group running other operations, for example bourse operations," the finance ministry said in the budget proposal.
"The development could lead to the state having a continued ownership interest in some of the central operations in the financial sector."
OM's chief executive Per E Larsson described the move as clear and powerful.

"It is positive if it facilitates a merger," Larsson told Reuters. "OM, the Stockholm Stock Exchange and VPC are important parts of the transaction chain and if it can be made more efficient through a merger that is positive."
Larsson added, however, that OM needed to analyse the new situation.
VPC's chief executive Anders Reveman declined to comment on what he saw as an ownership issue.
VPC has not been involved in merger talks previously as it had not taken any initiatives to join the discussions and three-party negotiations would be more complex, Larsson said.
But the government preparing to act could cause problems, Hansson said.
"There is a conflict of goals, so negotiations could take time," Hansson said. "OM's shareholders have business goals and the government has national economic goals."
Larsson said, however, it was positive that the state wanted to get influence through ownership rather than through legislation.
"Ownership is the natural way to get influence and then the government also has to see to that we have laws that allow a competitive infra-structure," Larsson said.
The head of the Stockholm bourse, Bengt Ryden, told Reuters in December 1996 that he expected a merger of the bourse, OM and VPC.
"This would mean dynamic advantages because an integrated market probably is more attractive," he said.
Neither Ryden nor his deputy were available on Wednesday.
